claims.text: Solid-solution hardening driven by lattice distortion is the dominant factor governing hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
A heterogeneous mixture of atomic sizes increases lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion more effectively.
More effective obstruction of dislocation motion raises yield strength and hardness.
Composition can be varied to adjust lattice distortion while retaining similar phase stability and grain structure.
Using identical processing conditions minimizes extrinsic differences such as grain-size variation and secondary-phase formation.
Atomic-size mismatch, such as the standard deviation of constituent atomic radii, can quantify lattice distortion.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can be used to quantify lattice distortion or lattice strain.
Lattice distortion creates an irregular potential-energy landscape.
The irregular potential-energy landscape obstructs dislocation glide.
Obstruction from lattice distortion increases the activation energy for dislocation movement.
An increased activation energy for dislocation movement enhances yield strength and hardness through solid-solution strengthening.
Single-phase HEAs with greater quantified lattice distortion will have statistically significantly greater hardness than a minimally distorted baseline alloy.
Single-phase HEAs with greater quantified lattice distortion will have statistically significantly greater yield strength than a minimally distorted baseline alloy.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase HEAs processed under uniform conditions and compositions that avoid secondary phases.
Grain-boundary strengthening, processing-induced defects, or dispersion strengthening may dominate or mask the effect of lattice distortion.
A controlled series should vary quantified lattice distortion while holding processing, grain size, phase purity, and compositional homogeneity as constant as possible.
Failure of higher-distortion samples to show statistically significant increases in both hardness and yield strength relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
